title: Revisiting Visual Representation Enhancement of VLMs via Kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis

paper.title: Revisiting Visual Representation Enhancement of VLMs via Kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis
paper.abstract: Abstract Vision-language models such as CLIP exhibit strong semantic generalization, but remain limited in fine-grained visual perception. A recent work named KUEA presents a natural remedy by finetuning the image encoder under the supervision of the vision-centric DINOv2 to align their kernel matrices element-wisely, while regularizing the embeddings to remain close to the pretrained visual encoder for preserving image-text semantics in CLIP. However, we show that diminishing the role of the alignment loss to DINOv2 does not necessarily degrade its fine-grained visual performance, suggesting that the kernel-matrix discrepancy may be insufficient for further visual representation enhancement, motivating us to revisit the alignment formulation. In this work, we present a novel perspective to characterize representation alignment on feature subspaces through Kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis (KCCA), which maximizes the projection correlations. In optimization, we derive an efficient end-to-end training scheme upon KKT conditions, avoiding the eigenvalue problem in KCCA. Further, we extend our method into a 3-view formulation, i.e., 3vKCCA, in which the projections from the pretrained text encoder are also incorporated under a unified optimization framework for joint alignment. With CLIP ViT-L/14 on ImageNet-1K, our 3vKCCA improves the MMVP-VLM accuracy from 17.8 17.8 to 25.9 25.9 , substantially outperforming the existing methods, and meanwhile maintains zero-shot image–text retrieval performance.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Vision–Language Models (VLMs) have been attracting tremendous attention in recent years thanks to their strong semantic generalization in various downstream tasks [ 11 , 12 , 16 ] . Notably, the Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) model [ 15 ] demonstrates strong zero-shot recognition capabilities by aligning visual representations with textual descriptions. However, such contrastive pretraining does not necessarily encourage the visual encoder to capture finer pixel-level details, such as spatial relations, even when these details are readily distinguishable to human observers [ 18 ] . Vision-only self-supervised models such as DINOv2 [ 13 ] focus on visual representations that capture fine details with strong visual grounding, making them suitable supervisors for refining the visual encoder in CLIP. A key challenge naturally arises: how to enhance the visual representation without downgrading the image–text alignment of the pretrained VLM model. A recent work, KUEA [ 9 ] , proposes to balance these two goals with a weighted combination objective. KUEA minimizes an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm loss for visual alignment between two kernel matrices computed from embeddings of the finetuned visual encoder and DINOv2, and also regularizes an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm term to confine the finetuned visual embeddings close to the pretrained counterparts in CLIP for image-text pairing semantics. We revisit the kernel-alignment loss in KUEA by examining a premise underlying this formulation: whether and how the fine-grained visual capability benefits from the minimization of such alignment loss . We examine this premise on MMVP-VLM [ 18 ] , a benchmark for assessing fine-grained visual abilities. In our reproduction, removing the kernel-alignment loss from KUEA yields similar MMVP-VLM accuracy as the full objective; when further minimizing the alignment loss and meanwhile downweighting the regularization term, the fine-grained visual performance does not improve either. This observation indicates that (i) the continual training with the regularization term may also contribute to enhancing visual capabilities, and (ii) the optimization upon this kernel-alignment loss with DINOv2 can be insufficient for further enhancing fine-grained visual capabilities. We notice that a concurrent work, namely KALE [ 14 ] , partially addresses the above issues through a loss-equilibration controller that rescales the kernel-alignment loss towards a desired ratio over the regularization term for pronouncing the alignment to DINOv2. We go beyond the loss of straightforwardly approaching the kernel matrix from DINOv2, and also reconsider the maintenance of image-text semantics in the pretrained CLIP from the role of the text encoder under a unified framework. In this work, we present a novel perspective that characterizes the representation alignment on feature subspaces through Kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis (KCCA) [ 2 , 17 ] . Under our framework, the alignment is formulated by the maximal correlations between the representation projections of the finetuned visual encoder and DINOv2. KCCA has long been considered a fundamental tool to identify projection directions, along which cross-view variations are maximally associated. The couplings in KCCA are celebrated with explicit optimization formulas and theoretical guarantees [ 2 , 10 ] , in contrast to the existing kernel-alignment loss of straightforwardly minimizing element-wise distances. Furthermore, we resort to the projections of the pretrained text encoder from CLIP and incorporate them into the alignment under our KCCA-based framework with a 3-view extension, namely 3vKCCA. Then, a joint optimization problem is established, which finetunes the image encoder of CLIP to align not only with the supervision of DINOv2 for enhancing fine-grained visual capabilities, but also with the frozen text encoder from CLIP for preserving image–text semantics. Experiments on OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14 show that our 3vKCCA distinctively improves fine-grained visual capabilities on MMVP-VLM from 17.8 to 25.9, while preserving strong zero-shot image–text retrievals of the pretrained CLIP. We then further investigate our perspective upon subspace projection correlations for representation alignment. Firstly, ablation studies show that our performance gain diminishes when the KCCA-alignment loss to DINOv2 is removed, when the correspondence to DINOv2 is shuffled, or when DINOv2 is replaced by a random teacher model for supervision; these results verify that the fine-grained visual capabilities indeed benefit from our alignment formulation. Secondly, our 3-view KCCA extension leveraging the frozen text encoder consistently outperforms the 2-view alternative; this reveals that upon aligning to strong visual supervision, visual representations are promising to be enhanced via cross-view couplings complemented by text semantics.

sections.heading: Enhancing Visual Representations of CLIP.
sections.text: Prior work considers the enhancement of fine-grained visual representations of VLMs mainly by localized supervision or vision-centric teacher models. RegionCLIP learns from region–text pairs [ 25 ] , whereas FG-CLIP combines detailed captions, region annotations, and hard negatives [ 22 ] . CLIP-DINOiser transfers DINO-derived localization priors to CLIP [ 21 ] , and Talk2DINO maps CLIP text embeddings to DINOv2 patch features [ 4 ] . More closely related to image-only finetuning as addressed in this work, DIVA uses diffusion feedback [ 20 ] , while KUEA matches the elements of kernel matrices from CLIP and DINOv2 [ 9 ] . Upon KUEA, KALE adaptively balances the reweighted loss terms for improved fine-grained visual capabilities [ 14 ] .

sections.heading: Kernel CCA and its Multi-View Extensions.
sections.text: Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) [ 10 ] learns linear projections that maximize correlation between a pair of views, i.e., two sources of data. Kernel CCA (KCCA) extends this principle to nonlinear relations through kernel tricks [ 2 , 17 , 19 ] . Deep CCA [ 1 ] parameterizes the nonlinear transformations with neural networks and [ 6 ] further derives generic deep CCA formulations together with their multi-view extensions. Some recent work considers connecting CCA to the training objectives of Barlow Twins [ 24 ] and VICReg [ 3 ] in large language models. Our work leverages Least Squares Support Vector Machines (LSSVM) [ 17 ] to formulate a KCCA-based objective over 3 functionally distinct views, where the stationary solutions with their Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions ensure a zero-value objective in an unconstrained optimization form, making it possible to be trained in an efficient end-to-end manner.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: In this section, we innovate to characterize the representation alignment through their projection correlations in feature subspaces under the KCCA framework to improve visual capabilities in CLIP. This perspective differs from the mainstream approach of minimizing sample-wise distances, e.g., the difference between the element-wise discrepancy of two kernels in KUEA or even the contrastive loss in pretraining CLIP. Our work resorts to the alignment through the correlations in projected subspaces, in which maximal information couplings are guaranteed by the well-established KCCA method. An efficient end-to-end training scheme under KKT conditions is then proposed.

sections.heading: The 3-view KCCA Extension of Joint Alignment with Text Semantics.
sections.text: Under the KCCA framework, the two views can be flexibly extended with multiple ones, which are jointly optimized to maximize mutual correlations [ 5 , 6 , 17 ] . Our 2-view KCCA optimization to align with DINOv2 f dino f_{\rm{dino}} can be accordingly further developed to jointly align with the pretrained text encoder f txt f_{\rm{txt}} , i.e., the 3rd view, for preserving image-text pairing semantics in the pretrained CLIP. sections.heading: 3.2 An End-to-End Optimization Scheme
sections.text: In optimization, the parameters 𝜽 \bm{\theta} of the CLIP visual encoder f ^ img \hat{f}_{\rm{img}} are finetuned and the parameters in our 3vKCCA are also optimized. KCCA commonly solves a generalized eigenvalue problem in the dual form. However, in this post-training process, it is impractical to repeatedly solve a generalized eigenvalue problem during each iteration of finetuning the network parameters 𝜽 \bm{\theta} of the CLIP visual encoder f ^ img \hat{f}_{\rm{img}} . Thus, we resort to the optimization of 3vKCCA in the primal. In the following Lemma 1 , we prove the zero-value property of the primal optimization objective J J in ( 2 ), when it is evaluated at stationary solutions with the KKT conditions, as proved in Appendix A . Thus, the optimization of our method is cast in an efficient end-to-end manner with ( 3 ), where the eigenvalue problem related to KCCA optimization is avoided. Note that since the projection weight matrices W v W_{v} in 3vKCCA are low-dimensional, the additional computational overhead is negligible compared to the CLIP backbones.

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: In this section, we evaluate our 3vKCCA on fine-grained visual capabilities and the pretrained image-text retrievals, and also investigate which specific components contribute to performance gains.

sections.heading: 4.1 Setups
sections.text: We adopt OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14 and fine-tune its visual encoder on ImageNet-1K [ 8 ] , while keeping the text encoder frozen. A DINOv2 model with a ViT-L/14 backbone is used as the vision-centric supervisor. We evaluate fine-grained visual capabilities on MMVP-VLM [ 18 ] , which contains visually distinct image pairs that CLIP maps to nearby representations across nine visual patterns. We also report zero-shot image–text retrieval on Flickr30K [ 23 ] and MSCOCO [ 7 ] . Full implementation details are provided in Appendix C .

sections.heading: Main Results.
sections.text: As shown in Table 1 , our 3vKCCA improves the average MMVP-VLM accuracy from 17.8 17.8 to 25.9 25.9 , substantially outperforming DIVA and KUEA by 2.9 2.9 and 5.2 5.2 , respectively. In the meantime, we improve the aggregate retrieval score from 72.7 72.7 to 73.3 73.3 . These results verify the effectiveness of our 3vKCCA for enhancing fine-grained visual perception and retaining the image-text semantics in the pretrained CLIP. These ablation results attribute our visual representation enhancement to the projection correlations learned under DINOv2 supervision on subspaces with KCCA-based optimization. sections.heading: Investigation on Multi-view Setups.
sections.text: We then present ablation studies on the role of our deployed 3rd view that leverages the embedding projections from the frozen CLIP text encoder. Table 3 demonstrates that the 2-view KCCA-alignment to DINOv2 in Section 3.1 readily improves the MMVP accuracy from 20.7 20.7 to 23.0 23.0 , while incorporating the 3rd view of the pretrained CLIP text encoder further brings distinctive improvement to 25.9 25.9 . Note that when taking the pretrained CLIP image representations as the 3rd view, the MMVP accuracy remains at 20.7 20.7 . This is in sharp contrast to our deployment with the CLIP text encoder being the 3rd view, which brings distinctive improvements, revealing the potential of the complementary text semantics as done in our 3vKCCA for further enhancing visual representations.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion and Outlook
sections.text: We revisit the fine-grained visual representation enhancement of CLIP under vision-centric supervision from DINOv2. Beyond element-wise matching of induced kernel matrices, we align representations in feature subspaces by maximizing projection correlations through KCCA, and extend this alignment into a 3-view formulation by incorporating embeddings from the frozen CLIP text encoder, namely 3vKCCA. With the Lagrangian duality and the KKT conditions, we derive an efficient end-to-end training scheme based on a necessary condition satisfied by stationary solutions. Experiments demonstrate substantial gains on MMVP-VLM while preserving image-text semantics, with varied ablations validating our alignment scheme upon KCCA and its multi-view extension. Currently, our study is conducted under the CLIP-DINOv2 setups. It would be interesting and worthwhile to explore other VLM backbones, vision-centric teachers, and broader perceptual benchmarks in future work, which we hope could inspire further investigations on the potential of optimizing subspace projections for representation alignment in VLMs and beyond.

sections.heading: Remarks on Lemma 1 and our loss function.
sections.text: Lemma 1 establishes J ⋆ = 0 J^{\star}=0 as a necessary condition satisfied by stationary solutions of our 3vKCCA under the KKT conditions. For the total training loss of Eq. ( 3 ) in the main manuscript, we then use J 2 \sqrt{J^{2}} as the loss function associated with this zero-value property and minimize it jointly with the regularization term, which avoids the eigenvalue problem typically solved in KCCA and makes the training remain under the end-to-end setups as in pretraining or post-training generic neural networks.

sections.heading: Visualization on Losses during Training
sections.text: To complement the ablation results in Table 2 , we visualize the training losses of the alignment and regularization objectives for KUEA and 3vKCCA in Fig. 2 . For KUEA, the kernel-alignment loss oscillates within a relatively stable range throughout training and does not exhibit a clear downward trend. This optimization behavior is consistent with our ablation result that removing the KUEA alignment term leaves the MMVP performance unchanged. Together, these observations suggest that the kernel-alignment objective provides limited effective contribution under the considered training setup, motivating us to revisit the alignment formulation. For comparison, we also report the training losses of 3vKCCA under the KCCA-based alignment objective introduced in Sec. 3 . As shown in Fig. 2 , the alignment loss decreases rapidly during the early stage of training and then gradually converges to a low and relatively stable range. (a) KUEA: alignment loss. (b) KUEA: regularization loss. (c) 3vKCCA: alignment loss. (d) 3vKCCA: regularization loss. Figure 2 : Training dynamics of KUEA and 3vKCCA. The left and right columns show the alignment and regularization losses, respectively, for KUEA and 3vKCCA. In our implementation, the alignment and regularization losses are recorded as loss_align and loss_clean , respectively.

sections.heading: Feature Processing.
sections.text: For each view v ∈ 𝒱 = { V , D , T } v\in\mathcal{V}=\{V,D,T\} , we construct the feature representation ϕ v ( n ) \phi_{v}^{(n)} by applying sample-wise ℓ 2 \ell_{2} normalization followed by minibatch centering to the encoder embedding 𝒉 v ( n ) \bm{h}_{v}^{(n)} . Specifically, we conduct ϕ v ( n ) = 𝒉 v ( n ) ‖ 𝒉 v ( n ) ‖ 2 − 1 B ​ ∑ m ∈ ℬ 𝒉 v ( m ) ‖ 𝒉 v ( m ) ‖ 2 , \phi_{v}^{(n)}=\frac{\bm{h}_{v}^{(n)}}{\|\bm{h}_{v}^{(n)}\|_{2}}-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{\bm{h}_{v}^{(m)}}{\|\bm{h}_{v}^{(m)}\|_{2}}, (18) where ℬ \mathcal{B} denotes the current minibatch of size B B . The centering operation is performed separately for each view. The resulting features are therefore normalized at the sample level and centered within the current minibatch before being projected by W v W_{v} .

sections.heading: Practical Implementations in Optimization.
sections.text: During end-to-end training, we apply a post-update normalization to the canonical projection matrices associated with the two visual views. Specifically, for W v = [ 𝒘 v , 1 , … , 𝒘 v , r ] , v ∈ { V , D } , W_{v}=[\bm{w}_{v,1},\ldots,\bm{w}_{v,r}],\qquad v\in\{V,D\}, (19) after each optimizer update, we perform 𝒘 v , k ← 𝒘 v , k ‖ 𝒘 v , k ‖ 2 , v ∈ { V , D } , k = 1 , … , r , \bm{w}_{v,k}\leftarrow\frac{\bm{w}_{v,k}}{\left\|\bm{w}_{v,k}\right\|_{2}},\qquad v\in\{V,D\},\quad k=1,\ldots,r, (20) where r r is the projection dimension. This column-wise normalization controls the scale of the canonical directions in the alignment to DINOv2 during training. This also helps keep the scale of the two visual projection directions stable during training. We do not apply this normalization to W T W_{T} , leaving the text-view projection unconstrained to retain scale flexibility in cross-modal correlation optimization. For numerical stability, we implement the alignment objective as ℒ align = J 2 + ϵ , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}=\sqrt{J^{2}+\epsilon}, where J J is the three-view primal objective defined in the main text with ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} . The small constant ϵ \epsilon stabilizes both the loss value and its gradient when J J approaches zero, while preserving J = 0 J=0 as the zero-residual target. The regularization term follows the definition in the main text. The complete training objective is then cast as: ℒ = η ​ J 2 + ϵ + ℒ reg , \mathcal{L}=\eta\sqrt{J^{2}+\epsilon}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}, (21) with ℒ reg = 1 N ​ ∑ n = 1 N ‖ f ^ img ​ ( I ( n ) ) − f img ​ ( I ( n ) ) ‖ 2 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reg}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\|\hat{f}_{\mathrm{img}}\!\left(I^{(n)}\right)-f_{\mathrm{img}}\!\left(I^{(n)}\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}.

sections.text: We set the pairwise correlation weight to ρ = 5.0 \rho=5.0 and use γ V = γ D = γ T = 1.0 \gamma_{V}=\gamma_{D}=\gamma_{T}=1.0 for the three views. The number of canonical components is set to r = 8 r=8 . For the practical training objective, we weight the alignment term by η = 78.125 \eta=78.125 . We train the model using AdamW with a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} and a weight decay of 10 − 4 10^{-4} . Post-training is performed for 40,000 40{,}000 optimization steps with a batch size of 64 64 , including 2,800 2{,}800 warmup steps. All experiments use 2 × RTX 5090 GPUs.

Xiaoyu Liu 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Jian Sun Qinghua Tao † † thanks: Corresponding author. Email: qinghua.tao@bit.edu.cn Affiliation: Beijing Institute of Technology Abstract Vision-language models such as CLIP exhibit strong semantic generalization, but remain limited in fine-grained visual perception. A recent work named KUEA presents a natural remedy by finetuning the image encoder under the supervision of the vision-centric DINOv2 to align their kernel matrices element-wisely, while regularizing the embeddings to remain close to the pretrained visual encoder for preserving image-text semantics in CLIP. However, we show that diminishing the role of the alignment loss to DINOv2 does not necessarily degrade its fine-grained visual performance, suggesting that the kernel-matrix discrepancy may be insufficient for further visual representation enhancement, motivating us to revisit the alignment formulation. In this work, we present a novel perspective to characterize representation alignment on feature subspaces through Kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis (KCCA), which maximizes the projection correlations. In optimization, we derive an efficient end-to-end training scheme upon KKT conditions, avoiding the eigenvalue problem in KCCA. Further, we extend our method into a 3-view formulation, i.e., 3vKCCA, in which the projections from the pretrained text encoder are also incorporated under a unified optimization framework for joint alignment. With CLIP ViT-L/14 on ImageNet-1K, our 3vKCCA improves the MMVP-VLM accuracy from 17.8 17.8 to 25.9 25.9 , substantially outperforming the existing methods, and meanwhile maintains zero-shot image–text retrieval performance. 1 Introduction Vision–Language Models (VLMs) have been attracting tremendous attention in recent years thanks to their strong semantic generalization in various downstream tasks [ 11 , 12 , 16 ] . Notably, the Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) model [ 15 ] demonstrates strong zero-shot recognition capabilities by aligning visual representations with textual descriptions. However, such contrastive pretraining does not necessarily encourage the visual encoder to capture finer pixel-level details, such as spatial relations, even when these details are readily distinguishable to human observers [ 18 ] . Vision-only self-supervised models such as DINOv2 [ 13 ] focus on visual representations that capture fine details with strong visual grounding, making them suitable supervisors for refining the visual encoder in CLIP. A key challenge naturally arises: how to enhance the visual representation without downgrading the image–text alignment of the pretrained VLM model. A recent work, KUEA [ 9 ] , proposes to balance these two goals with a weighted combination objective. KUEA minimizes an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm loss for visual alignment between two kernel matrices computed from embeddings of the finetuned visual encoder and DINOv2, and also regularizes an ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm term to confine the finetuned visual embeddings close to the pretrained counterparts in CLIP for image-text pairing semantics. We revisit the kernel-alignment loss in KUEA by examining a premise underlying this formulation: whether and how the fine-grained visual capability benefits from the minimization of such alignment loss . We examine this premise on MMVP-VLM [ 18 ] , a benchmark for assessing fine-grained visual abilities. In our reproduction, removing the kernel-alignment loss from KUEA yields similar MMVP-VLM accuracy as the full objective; when further minimizing the alignment loss and meanwhile downweighting the regularization term, the fine-grained visual performance does not improve either. This observation indicates that (i) the continual training with the regularization term may also contribute to enhancing visual capabilities, and (ii) the optimization upon this kernel-alignment loss with DINOv2 can be insufficient for further enhancing fine-grained visual capabilities. We notice that a concurrent work, namely KALE [ 14 ] , partially addresses the above issues through a loss-equilibration controller that rescales the kernel-alignment loss towards a desired ratio over the regularization term for pronouncing the alignment to DINOv2. We go beyond the loss of straightforwardly approaching the kernel matrix from DINOv2, and also reconsider the maintenance of image-text semantics in the pretrained CLIP from the role of the text encoder under a unified framework. In this work, we present a novel perspective that characterizes the representation alignment on feature subspaces through Kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis (KCCA) [ 2 , 17 ] . Under our framework, the alignment is formulated by the maximal correlations between the representation projections of the finetuned visual encoder and DINOv2. KCCA has long been considered a fundamental tool to identify projection directions, along which cross-view variations are maximally associated. The couplings in KCCA are celebrated with explicit optimization formulas and theoretical guarantees [ 2 , 10 ] , in contrast to the existing kernel-alignment loss of straightforwardly minimizing element-wise distances. Furthermore, we resort to the projections of the pretrained text encoder from CLIP and incorporate them into the alignment under our KCCA-based framework with a 3-view extension, namely 3vKCCA. Then, a joint optimization problem is established, which finetunes the image encoder of CLIP to align not only with the supervision of DINOv2 for enhancing fine-grained visual capabilities, but also with the frozen text encoder from CLIP for preserving image–text semantics. Experiments on OpenAI CLIP ViT-L/14 show that our 3vKCCA distinctively improves fine-grained visual capabilities on MMVP-VLM from 17.8 to 25.9, while preserving strong zero-shot image–text retrievals of the pretrained CLIP. We then further investigate our perspective upon subspace projection correlations for representation alignment. Firstly, ablation studies show that our performance gain diminishes when the KCCA-alignment loss to DINOv2 is removed, when the correspondence to DINOv2 is shuffled, or when DINOv2 is replaced by a random teacher model for supervision; these results verify that the fine-grained visual capabilities indeed benefit from our alignment formulation. Secondly, our 3-view KCCA extension leveraging the frozen text encoder consistently outperforms the 2-view alternative; this reveals that upon aligning to strong visual supervision, visual representations are promising to be enhanced via cross-view couplings complemented by text semantics. 2 Related Work Enhancing Visual Representations of CLIP. Prior work considers the enhancement of fine-grained visual representations of VLMs mainly by localized supervision or vision-centric teacher models. RegionCLIP learns from region–text pairs [ 25 ] , whereas FG-CLIP combines detailed captions, region annotations, and hard negatives [ 22 ] . CLIP-DINOiser transfers DINO-derived localization priors to CLIP [ 21 ] , and Talk2DINO maps CLIP text embeddings to DINOv2 patch features [ 4 ] . More closely related to image-only finetuning as addressed in this work, DIVA uses diffusion feedback [ 20 ] , while KUEA matches the elements of kernel matrices from CLIP and DINOv2 [ 9 ] . Upon KUEA, KALE adaptively balances the reweighted loss terms for improved fine-grained visual capabilities [ 14 ] . Kernel CCA and its Multi-View Extensions. Canonical correlation analysis (CCA) [ 10 ] learns linear projections that maximize correlation between a pair of views, i.e., two sources of data. Kernel CCA (KCCA) extends this principle to nonlinear relations through kernel tricks [ 2 , 17 , 19 ] . Deep CCA [ 1 ] parameterizes the nonlinear transformations with neural networks and [ 6 ] further derives generic deep CCA formulations together with their multi-view extensions. Some recent work considers connecting CCA to the training objectives of Barlow Twins [ 24 ] and VICReg [ 3 ] in large language models. Our work leverages Least Squares Support Vector Machines (LSSVM) [ 17 ] to formulate a KCCA-based objective over 3 functionally distinct views, where the stationary solutions with their Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions ensure a zero-value objective in an unconstrained optimization form, making it possible to be trained in an efficient end-to-end manner. 3 Method In this section, we innovate to characterize the representation alignment through their projection correlations in feature subspaces under the KCCA framework to improve visual capabilities in CLIP. This perspective differs from the mainstream approach of minimizing sample-wise distances, e.g., the difference between the element-wise discrepancy of two kernels in KUEA or even the contrastive loss in pretraining CLIP. Our work resorts to the alignment through the correlations in projected subspaces, in which maximal information couplings are guaranteed by the well-established KCCA method. An efficient end-to-end training scheme under KKT conditions is then proposed. Notation. Beyond element-wise matching of induced kernel matrices, we align representations in feature subspaces by maximizing projection correlations through KCCA, and extend this alignment into a 3-view formulation by incorporating embeddings from the frozen CLIP text encoder, namely 3vKCCA. With the Lagrangian duality and the KKT conditions, we derive an efficient end-to-end training scheme based on a necessary condition satisfied by stationary solutions. Experiments demonstrate substantial gains on MMVP-VLM while preserving image-text semantics, with varied ablations validating our alignment scheme upon KCCA and its multi-view extension. Currently, our study is conducted under the CLIP-DINOv2 setups. It would be interesting and worthwhile to explore other VLM backbones, vision-centric teachers, and broader perceptual benchmarks in future work, which we hope could inspire further investigations on the potential of optimizing subspace projections for representation alignment in VLMs and beyond.
